title.en: The God-man with Two Natures: Osiris Incarnate
title.zh: 雙性之神人：化身之奧西里斯

region.en: Egypt, the theology of divine kingship (the Pharaoh's ancestor)
region.zh: 埃及神王神學（法老之祖）

texts.period: Classical sources assessed against 3000-year-old Egyptian texts (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I, 1911, ch. I)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. I, the god-man doctrine of Osiris

summary.en: Budge's central theological claim, drawn from Plutarch and Diodorus read against the oldest texts: both classical authors assign Osiris a divine origin and state that he reigned in the form of a man upon the earth, 'so it is clear that the Egyptians generally believed that a god made himself incarnate, and that an immediate ancestor of the first Pharaoh of Egypt was a being who possessed two natures, the one human and the other divine' — the mortal body alone suffered death, 'in the divinity and immortality of the god-man Osiris lay the strength of the power with which he appealed to the minds and hopes of the Egyptians for thousands of years.'
summary.zh: 伯奇之核心神學論，取普魯塔克與狄奧多羅斯對讀最古文本：二古典作家皆謂奧西里斯出身神聖、以人形王於地上——『故可斷言：埃及人一般信神曾自化其身，而埃及首位法老之直系祖先乃具雙性者，一屬人、一屬神』——死者僅其凡體；『神人奧西里斯之神聖與不朽，即其數千年感召埃及人心與希望之力之所在。』

sensitivity.note: Egyptological theology via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions. Budge's own comparison of the two-natures doctrine with Christian incarnational language is implicit in his framing.

passages.text: Both Plutarch and Diodorus agree in assigning a divine origin to Osiris, and both state that he reigned in the form of a man upon the earth. This being so it is clear that the Egyptians generally believed that a god made himself incarnate, and that an immediate ancestor of the first Pharaoh of Egypt was a being who possessed two natures, the one human and the other divine.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. I.

passages.text: As a man he performed the good works which his divine nature indicated to him, he abolished cannibalism, he improved the manners and morals of men, he taught them to live according to law, to worship the gods, and to practise the arts of agriculture. Filled with love for man he set out to travel over the whole world so that he might teach all non-Egyptians to embrace his beneficent doctrine, and enjoy the blessings which accrue to God-fearing and law-abiding peoples. This god-man was hated by his brother, who by a cunning device inveigled him into a box, which he closed and sealed with lead, and thus killed him.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. I.

passages.text: The divine part of Osiris did not die, it was only the mortal body, which he put on when he came from the abode of the gods to reign upon earth, that suffered death. In the divinity and immortality of the god-man Osiris lay the strength of the power with which he appealed to the minds and hopes of the Egyptians for thousands of years, and we shall see in the course of the following pages that both these conceptions of Osiris are of purely African origin, and that they were in existence long before the Dynastic Period in Egypt.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. I.

texts.language: Egyptian texts read through classical sources
texts.canonical_translation: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (London, 1911), ch. I

narrative.en:
What exactly did Egypt believe had happened to Osiris? Budge's first chapter frames the answer as a two-natures doctrine. Plutarch and Diodorus, whatever their confusions, agree on the essential points: Osiris was of divine origin and 'reigned in the form of a man upon the earth' — from which Budge draws the far-reaching conclusion that 'the Egyptians generally believed that a god made himself incarnate, and that an immediate ancestor of the first Pharaoh of Egypt was a being who possessed two natures, the one human and the other divine.'

As a man, this god-man 'performed the good works which his divine nature indicated to him' — abolished cannibalism, improved the manners and morals of men, taught law, worship and agriculture — and then, 'filled with love for man', set out to teach the whole world. His brother's cunning box killed only what was mortal in him. The body that went into the river and floated to the reed marshes was the mortal body 'which he put on when he came from the abode of the gods to reign upon earth'; the divine part did not die. Hence the possibility that Plutarch records and the Pyramid Texts confirm: that Osiris returned from the Other World, spoke, and appeared 'in a form which Horus could recognize' — a spirit, or his own body raised, Budge leaves open, but with 'the power of speech and thought'.

The payoff, for Budge, is historical: 'in the divinity and immortality of the god-man Osiris lay the strength of the power with which he appealed to the minds and hopes of the Egyptians for thousands of years' — and both conceptions, the divine man and the risen body, are, he argues, 'of purely African origin', older than the Dynastic Period. The narrative material Plutarch gathered can be substantiated, piece by piece, 'by texts written three thousand years before the Christian Era', though the classical writers 'are arranged in wrong order' and joined in ways their informants could no longer understand. The god-man of Egypt is thus the through-line from the predynastic grave to the Passion Play of Abydos: a god who wore a body, died in it, and rose to rule the dead — and whose royal successors on earth each put on, at their coronation, the same two natures.

THE PHARAONIC CONSEQUENCE. The doctrine has a political edge that Budge makes explicit only by implication: if an immediate ancestor of the first Pharaoh was a god incarnate, then every Pharaoh who sat on the throne renewed the incarnation — the living king as Horus, the dead king as Osiris, both wearing the two natures. This is why the Osiris funerary texts are royal texts at their oldest, and why the god's rise tracks the king's: the Passion Play at Abydos rehearses annually the passion of the first god-man, the corn-mummy of Denderah buries and raises him in grain, and the ancestor stele of every village eventually puts his figure where the family's dead used to sit. The classical testimony, checked clause by clause against texts three thousand years older, thus confirms rather than distorts the native theology — it is the native theology, seen through Greek eyes, 'arranged in wrong order' but substantiated in nearly every part. For Budge the two-natures Osiris is the master-key of Egyptian religion: a god who wore a body, died in it, rose from it, and left the risen body as the pattern for every mummy laid in the tombs of Egypt.

functions: Theology of incarnation: the Pharaoh as successor to a god who wore two natures, human and divine
Soteriology: the mortal body alone died; the divine part survived — the ground of every Egyptian hope of rising
Source-critical method: testing Plutarch and Diodorus clause by clause against 3000-year-old texts

title.en: Byblos Is a Reed Marsh: A Philological Rescue of the Myth
title.zh: 比布魯斯本為蘆葦之沼：神話之語文校正

region.en: The papyrus marshes of the eastern Delta, Egypt (the true destination of the coffin)
region.zh: 埃及東三角洲紙莎草沼（棺槨真正漂至之地）

texts.period: Budge's source-critique of Plutarch, De Iside 15-18 (1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. I, the Byblos question

summary.en: Did the coffin really sail to Phoenicia? Budge argues not: 'The events which are stated by Plutarch to have happened to the body in this place are, clearly, interpolations of a comparatively late period, and were, I believe, invented to explain the similarity of the popular worship of Byblos with that of Osiris. Where the box was carried seems beyond doubt to have been the papyrus swamps... Byblos is a well-known word for the papyrus plant, and some copyist, who knew nothing of the fact that the Delta was full of papyrus marshes, concluded that the word in his text referred to the town of Byblos.'
summary.zh: 棺果真遠航腓尼基耶？伯奇以為否：『普魯塔克所述之事，顯為較晚之增插，蓋為解釋比布魯斯民俗與奧西里斯祭之相似而設；箱之所漂，無疑為紙莎草沼……Byblos（比布魯斯）本為紙莎草之通名；有抄工不知三角洲遍地莎草，遂誤以文中之字指腓尼基之比布魯斯城，而大改其傳說。』

sensitivity.note: Egyptological philology via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions. Modern scholarship is divided; the record preserves Budge's argument.

passages.text: The events which are stated by Plutarch to have happened to the body in this place are, clearly, interpolations of a comparatively late period, and were, I believe, invented to explain the similarity of the popular worship of Byblos with that of Osiris. Where the box was carried seems beyond doubt to have been the papyrus swamps, or the reedy marshes in the east of the Delta. Byblos is a well-known word for the papyrus plant, and some copyist, who knew nothing of the fact that the Delta was full of papyrus marshes, concluded that the word in his text referred to the town of Byblos, and so modified the legend considerably.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. I.

passages.text: Now, the well-known legend cut on the Metternich Stele says that Isis brought forth her son Horus among the papyrus swamps, and that she reared him there herself, therefore there must be some confusion in the sources of Plutarch's information. At all events, Isis seems to have left the box for some reason, and during her absence Typhon found it, dragged out the body of Osiris, and tore it into fourteen pieces, which he scattered about the country.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. I.

title.en: The Sceptre with the Eye: Osiris as the Sun in Hieroglyph
title.zh: 嵌目之杖：象形文字中之日神奧西里斯

region.en: Egypt, the writing system of the gods (symbolic pin, Heliopolis)
region.zh: 埃及神聖文字（象徵定位，赫利奧波利斯）

texts.period: Macrobius (5th century CE) and Diodorus, via Budge 1911

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. I, the hieroglyph of Osiris as the sun

summary.en: The solar reading of Osiris, from Macrobius: 'nor is it a secret that Osiris is nothing else than the sun, and Isis nothing else than the earth... whenever the Egyptians wish to express Osiris as the sun in their hieroglyphic letters they engrave a sceptre, and in it the form of an eye, and by this sign they show Osiris, signifying that this god is the sun, and that, with regal power raised on high, he looks down upon all things.'
summary.zh: 馬克羅比烏斯之日神讀法：『無可諱言：奧西里斯非他，即日也；伊西斯非他，即土也……埃及人欲於聖書中表日神奧西里斯，則刻一杖，杖中作目形——以此符號示彼神即日，以王者之權居高臨下、俯視萬有。』

sensitivity.note: Classical reading of hieroglyphs via Budge 1911 (quoting Macrobius, Saturnalia I); no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Macrobius, who flourished in the first half of the fifth century A.D., held the view that Osiris was the sun and Isis the earth. In proof of his assertion that Osiris is the sun he says that the Egyptians represent this god in their hieroglyphs under the form of a sceptre with an eye in it, and that they indicate by this the idea of the god surveying the universe from his exalted throne in the sky.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. I.

passages.text: Nor is it a secret that Osiris is nothing else than the sun, and Isis nothing else than the earth... Whenever the Egyptians wish to express Osiris as the sun in their hieroglyphic letters they engrave a sceptre, and in it the form of an eye, and by this sign they show Osiris, signifying that this god is the sun, and that, with regal power raised on high, he looks down upon all things.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. I, translating Macrobius, Saturnalia I.

title.en: The Spirit Burial: Isis' Formula for Making the Spirit of Osiris
title.zh: 靈之安葬：伊西斯塑奧西里斯之靈之咒

region.en: Abydos, Egypt (recited at every festival of Osiris, 22nd-26th of Khoiak)
region.zh: 埃及阿拜多斯（奧西里斯祭日誦之，荷阿克月22-26日）

texts.period: Paris papyrus, Graeco-Roman copy of Osiris liturgy (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II, 1911, ch. XVI)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XVI, the Spirit Burial of Osiris

summary.en: The rubric of the Osiris liturgy in full: the formula 'shall make glorious his soul, it shall stablish his body, it shall make his soul to shine in the sky, and shall make him to renew his youth each month, it shall stablish his son Horus upon his coffer' — recited by Isis and her sister Nephthys and also by her son Horus; 'it will benefit a man if he reciteth it, for he shall become a favoured one of Osiris upon earth among the living' — and in the litany Isis snares Set 'like a goose', kindling a lamp at the door of the urit chamber.
summary.zh: 奧西里斯禮文之眉批全篇：此咒『使其靈榮耀、堅其身、使其靈輝於天、使其月月復其青春、堅其子荷魯斯於其棺之上』——由伊西斯與其妹奈芙蒂斯及其子荷魯斯誦之；『人誦之則受益，必於世間為奧西里斯所眷』——禮文中伊西斯於烏瑞特室門前燃燈，『以網捕塞特如捕鵝』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient liturgical rubric via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The formula for making the spirit of Osiris in Akertet, which shall be made (i.e., recited) for this god, the Lord of Abydos, at every festival of Osiris, and at every appearance [of the god] in the temples. It shall make glorious his soul, it shall stablish his body, it shall make his soul to shine in the sky, and shall make him to renew his youth each month, it shall stablish his son Horus upon his coffer. This formula was recited by the sister [of the god]. It will benefit a man if he reciteth it, for he shall become a favoured one of Osiris upon earth among the living; his son shall be established in his house every day, and his children upon the earth.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XVI, the rubric of the Spirit Burial.

passages.text: This formula was recited by Isis and her sister Nephthys, and also by her son Horus. And if it be recited for Osiris, it will cause the soul of the deceased to live in Akertet every day, it will gladden his heart, and will overthrow all his enemies; and it shall be recited during the IVth month of the season Akhet, from the XXIInd day to the XXVIth day thereof.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XVI, the rubric continued.

passages.text: Hail, Seker-Osiris! This calamity happened to thee in the primeval time. There have been made for thee mighty chambers in Tettu (Busiris). The god Utekh embalmed thee and made sweet the smell of thee. The god Anpu (Anubis) toiled for thee in the place of purification, and performed all the things which he had to perform. I and my sister Nephthys kindled a lamp at the door of the urit chamber, so that [we] might snare in a net Set like a goose. Anubis came forth from the place of purification and overthrew all thine enemies.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XVI, the litany of Isis.

title.en: The Heart, the Weigher of All: Ab Before the Scales
title.zh: 心，萬行之衡：天秤前之阿布

region.en: The Hall of Maati, Egyptian Other World

texts.period: Book of the Dead chs. 26-30B and 125 (Budge, The Book of the Dead, 1901, ch. VII)

source.work: The Book of the Dead, by E. A. Wallis Budge (1901), ch. VII, 'The Judgment of Osiris' (the heart ab)

summary.en: What is weighed at the Great Judgment: 'The heart, ab, was taken as the symbol of all the emotions, desires, and passions, both good and evil, and out of it proceeded the issues of life. It was intimately connected with the ka, i.e., the double or personality of a man, and several short spells in the Book of Coming Forth by Day were composed to ensure its preservation (Chapters XXVI-XXXB)' — the organ on which the whole verdict turned.
summary.zh: 大審判所秤者何：『心（ab）乃一切情感、欲念與激情——善惡皆然——之符號，生命之諸流皆出於其中；其與卡（人之兩重者）密切相連；故《來日之書》中若干短咒（第二六至三十B章）專為保其不失而作』——此器官繫全案之判。

sensitivity.note: Ancient doctrine via Budge 1901; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The heart, ab, was taken as the symbol of all the emotions, desires, and passions, both good and evil, and out of it proceeded the issues of life. It was intimately connected with the ka, i.e., the double or personality of a man, and several short spells in the Book Coming Forth by Day were composed to ensure its preservation (Chapters XXVI-XXXB). The great Chapter of the Judgment of Osiris, the CXXVth, is divided into three parts, which are sometimes (as in the Papyrus of Ani) prefaced by a Hymn to Osiris.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, The Book of the Dead (1901), ch. VII.

title.en: The Temple in the Water: Bubastis and Its Sacred Grove
title.zh: 水中之廟：布巴斯提斯與其聖林

region.en: Bubastis, Nile Delta, Egypt (the temple of Bastet, Artemis of the Greeks)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲布巴斯提斯（貝斯特神廟，希臘人之阿爾忒彌斯）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.138 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 138

summary.en: The temple everyone could look down upon: Bubastis stands raised on embankments thrown up by centuries of corvee labour — 'Except the entrance it is completely surrounded by water; for channels come in from the Nile... each a hundred feet broad and shaded over with trees; and the gateway has a height of ten fathoms, and it is adorned with figures six cubits high'; within runs a grove of very large trees planted round the temple-house where the image of the goddess stands, and a paved road of three furlongs leads east 'to the temple of Hermes.'
summary.zh: 人人可俯視之神廟：布巴斯提斯因數世勞役築堤而高——『除入口外，廟四面皆水；運河自尼羅引入……各寬百尺，兩岸有樹蔭蔽；門樓高十噚，飾以六肘之神像』；廟內繞大樹成林，環女神之室；更有一三弗隆石路向東『通赫耳墨斯之廟』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient travel description via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In this city there is a temple very well worthy of mention, for though there are other temples which are larger and built with more cost, none more than this is a pleasure to the eyes. Now Bubastis in the Hellenic tongue is Artemis, and her temple is ordered thus: — Except the entrance it is completely surrounded by water; for channels come in from the Nile, not joining one another, but each extending as far as the entrance of the temple, one flowing round on the one side and the other on the other side, each a hundred feet broad and shaded over with trees; and the gateway has a height of ten fathoms, and it is adorned with figures six cubits high, very noteworthy.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.138.

passages.text: This temple is in the middle of the city and is looked down upon from all sides as one goes round, for since the city has been banked up to a height, while the temple has not been moved from the place where it was at the first built, it is possible to look down into it: and round it runs a stone wall with figures carved upon it, while within it there is a grove of very large trees planted round a large temple-house, within which is the image of the goddess: and the breadth and length of the temple is a furlong every way. Opposite the entrance there is a road paved with stone for about three furlongs, which leads through the market-place towards the East, with a breadth of about four hundred feet; and on this side and on that grow trees of height reaching to heaven: and the road leads to the temple of Hermes.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.138.

title.en: The Pine Trunk of Isis: A Roman-Egyptian Funeral Rite
title.zh: 伊西斯之松：羅馬-埃及葬儀

region.en: The Isis temples of the Roman Empire (the annual rite of the pine)
region.zh: 羅馬帝國之伊西斯神廟（松木歲儀）

texts.period: Recorded by Firmicus Maternus (4th century CE), quoted in Budge 1911

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. I, the rite of the pine of Isis

summary.en: The Egyptian mystery rite as Rome practised it, in Firmicus Maternus' testimony: 'In the sacred rites of Isis a trunk is cut from a pine tree; the middle part of this trunk is hollowed out with skill; into it an image of Osiris made of reeds is buried' — the same trunk, and the other woods of the rite, 'a flame consumes; for even after a year the fire of the pyre feeds upon those very logs.'
summary.zh: 羅馬所行之埃及秘儀，菲爾米庫斯證之：『於伊西斯聖儀中，自松樹斬一幹；其幹之中段精巧鑿空；以葦製之奧西里斯小像葬於其中』——此幹與儀中諸木，『火焰盡焚之；歲餘，火仍食其薪』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient mystery-rite testimony via Budge 1911 (translating Firmicus, De errore profanarum religionum); no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In the sacred rites of Isis a trunk is cut from a pine tree. The middle part of this trunk is hollowed out with skill. Into it an image of Osiris made of reeds is buried. And the other woods also, which I have mentioned, a similar flame consumes; for even after a year the fire of the pyre feeds upon those very logs.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. I, translating Firmicus Maternus, De errore profanarum religionum (Latin quoted in Budge's footnote).
